questions.enonce_markdown: What is a redox reaction? *[1 mark]*
questions.corrige_markdown: A **redox reaction** is a reaction in which **oxidation and reduction take place together**: one species loses electrons (its oxidation number increases) while another species gains those electrons (its oxidation number decreases). The electrons lost by the reducing agent are exactly the electrons gained by the oxidising agent.

questions.enonce_markdown:
$31.0\ \mathrm{cm^3}$ of an acidified $\mathrm{KMnO_4}$ solution was required to completely oxidize $50\ \mathrm{cm^3}$ of $0.25\ \mathrm{M}$ solution of oxalic acid ($\mathrm{H_2C_2O_4}$). The unbalanced ionic equation is:

$\mathrm{C_2O_4^{2-}(aq) + MnO_4^{-}(aq) + H^{+}(aq) \rightarrow Mn^{2+}(aq) + CO_2(g) + H_2O(l)}$

(i) Write down the half equation for

A: Oxidation:

B: Reduction:

(ii) Write down the overall balanced equation

(iii) Calculate the concentration of the $\mathrm{KMnO_4}$ solution. *[5 marks]*
questions.corrige_markdown:
**(i) Half equations.**

A: Oxidation (carbon goes from $+3$ in oxalate to $+4$ in $\mathrm{CO_2}$): $\mathrm{C_2O_4^{2-}} \rightarrow 2\mathrm{CO_2} + 2\mathrm{e^{-}}$

B: Reduction (manganese goes from $+7$ to $+2$): $\mathrm{MnO_4^{-}} + 8\mathrm{H^{+}} + 5\mathrm{e^{-}} \rightarrow \mathrm{Mn^{2+}} + 4\mathrm{H_2O}$

Charge check: A: $-2 = 0 + 2(-1)$. B: left $-1 + 8 - 5 = +2$, right $+2$.

**(ii) Overall equation.** Multiply A by 5 and B by 2 so that 10 electrons are lost and gained, then add and cancel the electrons:

$5\mathrm{C_2O_4^{2-}} + 2\mathrm{MnO_4^{-}} + 16\mathrm{H^{+}} \rightarrow 10\mathrm{CO_2} + 2\mathrm{Mn^{2+}} + 8\mathrm{H_2O}$

Check: atoms C 10 = 10, O $20 + 8 = 28$ and $20 + 8 = 28$, H 16 = 16; charge $-10 - 2 + 16 = +4$ and $+4$.

**(iii) Concentration of the permanganate.**

Moles of oxalic acid (oxalate) $= \dfrac{50}{1000} \times 0.25 = 0.0125\ \mathrm{mol}$.

From the equation, $5\ \mathrm{C_2O_4^{2-}}$ react with $2\ \mathrm{MnO_4^-}$, so

moles of $\mathrm{MnO_4^-} = 0.0125 \times \dfrac{2}{5} = 0.00500\ \mathrm{mol}$.

This amount is contained in $31.0\ \mathrm{cm^3}$, so

$[\mathrm{KMnO_4}] = \dfrac{0.00500}{31.0/1000} = 0.161\ \mathrm{mol\ dm^{-3}}$.

**Concentration of $\mathrm{KMnO_4}$ = 0.161 M** (3 significant figures).

questions.enonce_markdown:
Bond energy can provide information about the energy changes that accompany a chemical reaction.

(i) What do you understand by the term bond energy?

(ii) The table below shows some average bond enthalpies

| Bond | Average bond enthalpy/$\mathrm{kJ\,mol^{-1}}$ |
|---|---|
| C - C | 350 |
| C = C | 610 |
| H - H | 436 |
| C - H | 410 |

A: Use this information to calculate the enthalpy change for the process

![fig-1](gce-al-chemistry-2025-p2-officiel-cameroun_exercice_1_fig_1.png)

(ethene plus hydrogen giving ethane: $\mathrm{CH_2{=}CH_2 + H{-}H \rightarrow CH_3{-}CH_3}$)

B: The enthalpy change of this reaction was found by experiment to be $-136\ \mathrm{kJ\,mol^{-1}}$. Explain why this value is different from that calculated above. *[4 marks]*
questions.corrige_markdown:
**(i) Bond energy (bond enthalpy)** is the energy required to break **one mole of a particular covalent bond in gaseous molecules** (into gaseous atoms), measured in $\mathrm{kJ\,mol^{-1}}$. For a bond found in many compounds an **average (mean) value** is quoted. The same amount of energy is released when the bond is formed.

**(ii) A. Enthalpy change.** Reaction: $\mathrm{CH_2{=}CH_2(g) + H{-}H(g) \rightarrow CH_3{-}CH_3(g)}$.

Bonds broken (energy absorbed): one $\mathrm{C{=}C}$ and one $\mathrm{H{-}H}$:
$610 + 436 = +1046\ \mathrm{kJ\,mol^{-1}}$.

Bonds formed (energy released): one $\mathrm{C{-}C}$ and two new $\mathrm{C{-}H}$ (the four original $\mathrm{C{-}H}$ bonds of ethene are unchanged and cancel):
$350 + 2 \times 410 = 350 + 820 = 1170\ \mathrm{kJ\,mol^{-1}}$.

$$\Delta H = \sum E(\text{bonds broken}) - \sum E(\text{bonds formed}) = 1046 - 1170$$

**$\Delta H = -124\ \mathrm{kJ\,mol^{-1}}$** (exothermic).

**B. Why the experimental value ($-136$) differs.** Bond enthalpies in the table are **average values** taken over many different compounds, so they are not the exact energies of the particular bonds in ethene and ethane (the strength of a bond depends on the rest of the molecule). The calculation also treats all species as gases under standard conditions and ignores the real environment of the bonds. The experimental value is the true enthalpy change for this reaction, so it differs from the estimate based on average bond enthalpies.

questions.enonce_markdown:
(i) State Le Chatelier's Principle.

(ii) Consider the reaction

$\mathrm{2NO_2(g) \rightleftharpoons N_2O_4(g)}$  $\Delta H^{\ominus} = +58.1\ \mathrm{kJ\,mol^{-1}}$

How does an increase in temperature affect:

A. The equilibrium constant?

B. The equilibrium position? *[3 marks]*
questions.corrige_markdown:
**(i) Le Chatelier's Principle.** When a system in dynamic equilibrium is subjected to a change in conditions (concentration, pressure or temperature), the position of equilibrium shifts in the direction that **opposes (tends to cancel) the change** imposed.

**(ii) Effect of raising the temperature**, using the data as printed ($\Delta H^{\ominus} = +58.1\ \mathrm{kJ\,mol^{-1}}$, so the forward reaction is endothermic):

A. **The equilibrium constant $K_c$ (or $K_p$) increases.** For an endothermic forward reaction, $K$ increases with temperature (van 't Hoff relation); $K$ changes only with temperature.

B. **The equilibrium position shifts to the right**, in the endothermic direction that absorbs the added heat, so the proportion of $\mathrm{N_2O_4}$ increases.

Remark: in reality the dimerisation $2\mathrm{NO_2} \rightleftharpoons \mathrm{N_2O_4}$ is exothermic (about $-57\ \mathrm{kJ\,mol^{-1}}$); with that sign the answers would be reversed ($K$ decreases, position shifts to the left). The answers above follow the data printed in the question.

questions.enonce_markdown:
Use the data below, where appropriate to answer the following questions:

| | Standard Electrode Potential | $E^{\ominus}$/V |
|---|---|---|
| A | $\mathrm{Fe^{3+}(aq) + e^- \rightarrow Fe^{2+}(aq)}$ | +0.27 |
| B | $\mathrm{NO_3^-(aq) + 3H^+(aq) + 2e^- \rightarrow HNO_2(aq) + H_2O(l)}$ | +0.94 |
| C | $\mathrm{Cl_2(aq) + 2e^- \rightarrow 2Cl^-(aq)}$ | +1.36 |
| D | $\mathrm{Cr_2O_7^{2-}(aq) + 14H^+(aq) + 6e^- \rightarrow 2Cr^{3+}(aq) + 7H_2O(l)}$ | +1.33 |
| E | $\mathrm{S_2O_8^{2-}(aq) + 2e^- \rightarrow 2SO_4^{2-}(aq)}$ | +2.01 |

(i) From the table above, select the species which is the most powerful reducing agent.

(ii) Calculate the oxidation state of Chromium in $\mathrm{Cr_2O_7^{2-}}$.

(iii) Write a cell diagram for the reaction when A and D are coupled and calculate the emf of the cell. *[4 marks]*
questions.corrige_markdown:
**(i) Most powerful reducing agent.** A reducing agent is the **reduced form** of the couple with the **most negative (least positive) $E^{\ominus}$**, because it gives up electrons most readily. The lowest value in the table is $+0.27\ \mathrm{V}$ (couple A), so the most powerful reducing agent is **$\mathrm{Fe^{2+}(aq)}$**.

**(ii) Oxidation state of Cr in $\mathrm{Cr_2O_7^{2-}}$.** Let the oxidation state of Cr be $x$:

$2x + 7(-2) = -2 \Rightarrow 2x = +12 \Rightarrow x = +6$. **Chromium is $+6$.**

**(iii) Cell A + D.** The couple with the more positive $E^{\ominus}$ (D, $+1.33\ \mathrm{V}$) is reduced and forms the positive electrode; the couple with the less positive $E^{\ominus}$ (A, $+0.27\ \mathrm{V}$) is oxidised and forms the negative electrode:

negative electrode: $\mathrm{Fe^{2+} \rightarrow Fe^{3+} + e^-}$ (oxidation)
positive electrode: $\mathrm{Cr_2O_7^{2-} + 14H^+ + 6e^- \rightarrow 2Cr^{3+} + 7H_2O}$ (reduction)

Cell diagram (oxidation on the left, reduction on the right, platinum electrodes because both couples are in solution):

$$\mathrm{Pt\,|\,Fe^{2+}(aq),\,Fe^{3+}(aq)\,\|\,Cr_2O_7^{2-}(aq),\,H^+(aq),\,Cr^{3+}(aq)\,|\,Pt}$$

$E_{\text{cell}} = E^{\ominus}_{\text{positive}} - E^{\ominus}_{\text{negative}} = 1.33 - 0.27 = \mathbf{+1.06\ V}$ (using the printed values).

Remark: the usual data-book value for $\mathrm{Fe^{3+}/Fe^{2+}}$ is $+0.77\ \mathrm{V}$ (which would give $0.56\ \mathrm{V}$); the answer above uses the value printed in the question.
